To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) the rat has been a useful model in the discovery of novel genes involved in blood pressure regulation and that (2) genome-wide association studies and the study of rare monogenic forms of human hypertension have led to the identification of novel genes involved blood pressure regulation.
the genetics of essential hypertension has been studied in humans and in animal models, and that the results from both approaches have been combined in a novel and successful way.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the genetic factors that determine blood pressure variation in experimental models and in humans.
the identification of genes and genetic variants that contribute to the development of essential hypertension.
the identification of genes and pathways involved in hypertension, and the translation of these findings to human essential hypertension.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

we are now at a point where the genetics of human essential hypertension has made substantial progress and is likely to lead to the identification of novel genes and mechanisms contributing to human hypertension.
the genetics of hypertension is a rapidly progressing field, which will continue to do so in the future.
the genetic basis of essential hypertension is complex and that the genetic contribution to the disease is heterogeneous and variable between populations.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the genetics of hypertension has been transformed in the past few years and the future is bright.
we have contributed to the discovery of a number of novel genes and pathways involved in blood pressure control.

the study of hypertension in experimental animals has contributed significantly to the identification of genes involved in blood pressure regulation and that the identification of these genes has contributed to the understanding of the genetic basis for essential hypertension in humans.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the study of monogenetic forms of hypertension in animal models and the study of human essential hypertension are complementary approaches and together provide a better understanding of the genetic basis of hypertension and its pathophysiology.
there is no single hypertension gene, but a large number of genetic and environmental factors that contribute to blood pressures variability.

there is a need for a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying blood pressure control and the development of hypertension, which can be achieved through the use of animal models and functional studies of candidate genes.
